body.text: Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will hold the balance of power in the state for the next four years.
Labor and the Greens have again clashed over preferences on their how-to-vote cards, with each party accusing the other of helping the Liberals and One Nation.
The leaders are also out campaigning, with Ben Carroll promising to slash waiting times for trains and Jess Wilson speaking with voters in Wodonga.

Seats in focus: Dandenong

Dandenong is one of the oldest Victorian lower house seats. It was once a swinging seat that traded hands between the left and right of politics. The seat last elected a Liberal at the 1967 election, but since a by-election in 1969 has elected Labor MPs without interruption. The redrawing of boundaries in advance of the 2002 election saw the seat become ultra-safe for Labor and the party’s two-party preferred result peaked at 74 per cent in 2018.

The current Labor member is Gabrielle Williams, who succeeded former Bracks government minister John Pandazopoulos. Williams became a parliamentary secretary immediately after entering parliament in 2014 and entered the ministry after the 2018 election.

Williams has been touted as a future Labor leader. She ascended to the deputy leadership of the party after leading a delegation of Labor MPs to inform Jacinta Allan she had lost majority support in the caucus. Even the dimmest view of Labor’s prospects would not see Dandenong lost by the party and, as such, it seems likely Williams will be among Labor’s leadership team after this election.
More on CFMEU's influence on government at Big Build royal commission
Stephen Villella, the delivery director for the consortium behind the Gap Road level crossing removal project, has spent his morning giving evidence at the Big Build royal commission in Melbourne.
He's recounted a crucial meeting at the CFMEU's headquarters on June 7, 2022, after works had been stopped on a level crossing removal project at Sunbury.
"There was a bit of chitchat. Quite stunted."

Sitting opposite Villella were key CFMEU figures Paul Tzimas and Joe Myles, who made several "demands" for their preferred health and safety representatives, and traffic and labour hire firms on the site.
"The inference from Mr Myles was that CFMEU had a lot of influence within government and our participation and collaboration with them would help us in future work," he says.
Asked what he meant by future work, Villella responded with "Melbourne Airport Rail".
It's yet another account of the pivotal meeting, which has been detailed by several witnesses this week.

The commission heard that during this secret meeting, CFMEU officials indicated that contractors would be favoured to win major contracts like the Melbourne Airport Rail if they cooperated with the union, with officials intimating they had a "direct line" to Jacinta Allan's office.
Ben Carroll takes a trip on the Hurstbridge line

In keeping with his pledge to invest $100 million in improving train services across Melbourne, Premier Ben Carroll left the car in the garage this morning and took the Hurstbridge line to his press conference.
Joined by his wife, Fiona Rothville, Carroll sat opposite another couple and had a chance for a chat in the carriage.
The conversation topics jumped from AI to Carroll's family life and lunch recommendations.
The premier made sure to give his own recommendations for restaurants in the CBD along the way.
"You can't go wrong, the Shark Fin Inn, dumplings and trays coming around," he said.
The Shark Fin Inn in Melbourne's CBD is a known hangout for Victorian Labor powerbrokers and ministers.
Our state political reporters say over xiao long baos, pork rolls and prawn dumplings, many a factional plan has been hatched there.
The outgoing MPs who will not contest the election
Political parties are busy campaigning for seats this week, and also trying to introduce some new faces to their electorates.
Twenty sitting MPs will not be contesting the next election, including some high-profile retirements.

Former premier Jacinta Allan announced she would not contest her Bendigo East seat after being forced out of office in August, while former Liberal leader Michael O'Brien is also calling time on his political career.

Liberals pledge to invest in regional Victorian roads
Jess Wilson was still in Wodonga this morning and made her pitch to voters with a promise to fund a major local road.
The Coalition has promised $50.1 million to duplicate Beechworth Road, as part of a wider guarantee to allocate more funding to regional roads.
Wilson said regional Victorians told her they felt "forgotten" by the government when it came to infrastructure.
"The potholes, the state of our roads comes up in every single conversation," Wilson said. "And that's exactly why we will guarantee 25 per cent of new infrastructure spend into regional Victoria."

Seats in focus: Croydon

Croydon was created ahead of the 2014 election from the now-abolished seat of Kilsyth. Current Liberal member David Hodgett was elected as the member for Kilsyth in the 2006 election and transferred to Croydon when it was first contested. He served on the Liberal front bench continuously from 2010 to October 2025, and between 2014 and 2018 was deputy leader of the party under Matthew Guy. He announced in August 2025 that he would not contest the 2026 election.

The past two elections have been tight contests between the major parties, but at this election it is possible that the match-up will shift to being between the Liberals and One Nation rather than Labor.

Many of Croydon’s residents, about 15 per cent, are employed in blue-collar occupations, which polling suggests are favourable to One Nation. With Labor bracing for a lower vote, the preferences of its voters could determine which party — the Liberals or One Nation — will win the seat. Hodgett’s retirement adds further uncertainty as to how the votes for the three parties settle.
